## Overview {#overview}

Many datasets include text, such as movie titles, country names, and survey answers. In this chapter, you will use [`str_detect()`]{.glossary-term data-term="str_detect()"} to find text that matches a pattern and combine those results with `dplyr::filter()` to select rows. You will also search passages from a research-integrity article, count matching passages, and retrieve them to read in context.

By the end of Chapter 17 you will be able to:

- 🔍 Find matching text in row names and character columns with `str_detect()`.

- 🎯 Use word boundaries, alternation, and capitalization options to define a search pattern.

- 🧺 Combine text-matching results with `filter()` to select rows.

- 🔁 Use [`sapply()`]{.glossary-term data-term="sapply()"} and [`lapply()`]{.glossary-term data-term="lapply()"} to apply an operation to several objects or keywords.

- 📖 Build a keyword index, retrieve matching passages, and distinguish passage counts from word-occurrence counts.

Keep these goals in mind as you move through each section.

## Warm‑Up {#warmup}

What is `str_detect()`?

A [pattern]{.glossary-term data-term="Pattern"} describes what you want to find in text. The `string` argument supplies the text to search, and `pattern` supplies the matching rule.

📜 **The SYNTAX:** `str_detect(string, pattern, negate = FALSE)`

🎯 **Goal:** Use the help file to identify the arguments and the type of result returned.

```{r , eval=FALSE}
?str_detect    # Arguments and return value (logical)
```

🗣 **Comment:** What do the `string` and `pattern` arguments supply, and what type of result does the function return?

For each nonmissing text value, `str_detect()` returns `TRUE` if the pattern matches and `FALSE` otherwise. You can use those logical results to filter rows or find matching positions.

## Row‑name search {#row-name-search}

🎯 **Goal:** Find states whose names begin with `New`.

```{r , eval=FALSE}
View(USArrests)  # View USArrests dataset in RStudio viewer
row.names(USArrests)  # Check row names of USArrests dataset
```

```{r}
# ⚡ Code
New_states <- USArrests %>%
  filter(str_detect(row.names(USArrests), "^New"))
```

The `^` anchors the pattern to the beginning of each name. The assignment saves the selected rows as `New_states`.

✔️ In [Chapter 11](../05-openmindedness/ch11-dplyr-subsetting.html#single-condition), a comparison such as `mpg >= 25` returned logical results. Here, `str_detect()` tests text instead of comparing numbers. `filter()` still uses the results in the same way: it keeps rows where the test returns `TRUE`.

```{r}
# ✅ Check
row.names(New_states)
```

🗣 **Comment:** Which *New* states were found?

## Column search {#column-search}

The `movielens` data frame contains one row per rating, so a movie title can appear in many rows.

🎯 **Goal:** Keep rating rows whose movie title contains the whole word `Love`.

```{r , eval=FALSE}
View(movielens)
nrow(movielens) 
```

```{r}
# ⚡ Code
Love_films <- movielens %>%
  filter(str_detect(title, "\\bLove\\b"))
```

```{r}
# ✅ Check
nrow(Love_films)
```

🗣 **Comment:** This counts matching rating rows, not distinct movies. Why can the same movie contribute more than one row?

## Exact word match {#exact-word-match}

Inside a quoted R pattern, write `\\b` to specify a [word boundary]{.glossary-term data-term="Word boundary"}.

The `region` column in `murders` contains names such as `"Northeast"`, `"North Central"`, and `"South"`.

```{r , eval=FALSE}
?stringr::regex
```

[Regular expressions]{.glossary-term data-term="Regular expression"} describe text patterns using ordinary text and special symbols. `str_detect()` uses them by default; [`regex()`]{.glossary-term data-term="regex()"} lets you specify matching options such as whether capitalization matters.

📜 **The SYNTAX (basic):** `regex(pattern, ignore_case = FALSE, ...)`

🎯 **Goal:** Match text without requiring the same capitalization.

```{r}
# ⚡ Code
str_detect("HELLO", regex("hello", ignore_case = TRUE))
```

✅ **Check:** Inspect the logical result. Did the pattern match?

🗣 **Comment:** Here, `ignore_case = TRUE` allows uppercase and lowercase letters to match. This is [case-insensitive matching]{.glossary-term data-term="Case-insensitive matching"}. Use [case-sensitive matching]{.glossary-term data-term="Case-sensitive matching"} when capitalization matters to your search.

🎯 **Goal:** Keep rows whose region contains the whole word `South`.

```{r}
# ⚡ Code
South_states <- murders %>%
  filter(str_detect(region, regex("\\bSouth\\b")))
```

```{r}
# ✅ Check
nrow(South_states)
```

🗣 **Comment:** Word boundaries let `"\\bSouth\\b"` match the whole word `South`, but not the beginning of `Southampton`. The word can occur within a longer name; the entire name does not have to equal `South`.

🎯 **Goal:** Keep rows whose region contains the whole word `North` or `South`.

```{r}
# ⚡ Code
NS_states <- murders %>%
  filter(str_detect(region, regex("\\b(North|South)\\b")))
```

```{r}
# ✅ Check
nrow(NS_states)
```

🗣 **Comment:** Inside a pattern, `|` matches either alternative. This is [alternation]{.glossary-term data-term="Alternation"}. This pattern finds the whole word `North` or `South`, so it can match `North Central` but not `Northeast`.

✔️ You used `|` in [Chapter 10](../05-openmindedness/ch10-and-or-in.html#or) to combine logical tests. Inside `"\\b(North|South)\\b"`, it separates text alternatives: `North` or `South`. The OR idea is familiar, but here the symbol belongs to the quoted search pattern.

## Count Matches Quickly {#count-matches-quickly}

🎯 **Goal:** Store the four row counts in a numeric vector.

```{r}
# ⚡ Code
match_counts <- c(
  nrow(New_states),
  nrow(Love_films),
  nrow(South_states),
  nrow(NS_states)
)
```

```{r}
# ⚡ Add names to the counts.
names(match_counts) <- c("New_states", "Love_films", "South_states", "NS_states")

# ✅ Check
match_counts
```

Alternatively, use `sapply()` to count rows in each data frame.

📜 **The SYNTAX (basic):** `sapply(X, FUN, ...)`

`X` is the list or vector to work through, and `FUN` is the function to apply to each element.

```{r , eval=FALSE}
?sapply # sapply() applies a function to each element of a list or vector
```

🎯 **Goal:** Apply `nrow()` to each of the four data frames and collect the counts.

```{r}
# ⚡ Code
match_counts <- sapply(list(New_states, Love_films, South_states, NS_states), nrow)

# ✅ Check
match_counts
```

🗣 **Comment:** `list()` collects the four data frames, and `sapply()` applies `nrow` to each one. Here, it returns a vector of counts. This list is unnamed, so the resulting counts do not have the labels added above.

## Inspect the Corpus {#inspect-the-corpus}

A [corpus]{.glossary-term data-term="Corpus"} is a collection of text prepared for analysis. This chapter uses passages from *Value pluralism in research integrity* by Peels and colleagues (2019).

**Source:** Peels, R., de Ridder, J., Haven, T., & Bouter, L. (2019). Value pluralism in research integrity. *Research Integrity and Peer Review, 4*, Article 18. [Read the original article](https://doi.org/10.1186/s41073-019-0076-4).

The article is licensed under [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). For this activity, the publisher's web text was extracted, display spacing was normalized, and headings were joined to the next passage. Web controls and author contact details were excluded.

Each vector entry is one passage. The supplied text includes paragraphs, list items, notes, references, and source and license information. Searches include all these entries, not just the main article.

Download `Science_Values.rds` and save it in the same folder as the document you are creating for this chapter:

<a href="data/Science_Values.rds" download>Download Science_Values.rds</a>

🎯 **Goal:** Read the file into the `Science_Values` character vector.

```{r , eval=FALSE}
# ⚡ Code
Science_Values <- readRDS("Science_Values.rds")  # creates Science_Values
```

```{r include=FALSE}
# Book rendering uses the bundled data file; readers use the download above.
Science_Values <- readRDS("data/Science_Values.rds")
```

```{r}
# ✅ Check
length(Science_Values)   # number of passages in the supplied file
```

🗣 **Comment:** `length()` counts entries in this character vector, so it tells you the number of passages, not the number of words.

To inspect the first few passages in RStudio, run:

```{r , eval=FALSE}
head(Science_Values)
```

## Build a Keyword Index {#build-a-keyword-index}

A [keyword index]{.glossary-term data-term="Keyword index"} connects each keyword with the positions of passages that match it. `lapply()` lets us repeat the search for each keyword and keep the results in a list.

📜 **The SYNTAX (basic):** `lapply(X, FUN, ...)`

```{r , eval=FALSE}
?lapply  # lapply() applies a function to each element of a list or vector
```

🎯 **Goal:** Create the vector of keywords to search for.

```{r}
# ⚡ Code
Index_Words <- c("values", "norms", "integrity", "ethics", "bias", "trust", 
                 "transparency", "responsibility", "reproducibility", "evidence", 
                 "policy", "funding", "conflict")
```

The searches below use case-insensitive, whole-word matching. Some words may have no matches; an empty result means the pattern was not found in the supplied text.

In `function(w)`, `w` receives one keyword at a time. `paste0()` joins the word boundaries and keyword into a pattern. `str_detect()` tests each passage, and `which()` returns the positions of the matches. `lapply()` stores one result per keyword in a list.

🎯 **Goal:** Build the index and name each list element with its keyword.

```{r}
# ⚡ Code
Index <- lapply(Index_Words, function(w) {
  which(str_detect(Science_Values, regex(paste0("\\b", w, "\\b"),
                                         ignore_case = TRUE)))
})
```

```{r}
# ⚡ Code
names(Index) <- Index_Words

# ✅ Check
names(Index)
```

```{r}
# ✅ Check the index for "trust".
Index[["trust"]]  
```

```{r}
# ✅ Count the matching passages.
length(Index[["trust"]])
```

🗣 **Comment:** `Index[["trust"]]` contains matching passage positions. Its length counts matching passages, not individual occurrences of the word; one passage can contain it more than once.

## Preview Context Passages {#preview-context-lines}

🎯 **Goal:** Retrieve matching passages so you can read the words in context.

```{r}
# ⚡ Code
Science_Values[Index[["transparency"]]][1:2]   # first two transparency hits
```

```{r}
# ⚡ Code
# Retrieve all passages containing the whole word "trust"
trust_passages <- Science_Values[Index[["trust"]]]
```

✔️ In [Chapter 8](../04-autonomy/ch08-indexing.html#which-function), `which()` returned positions that you used to select rows. Here, `Index[["trust"]]` contains matching passage positions. The brackets in `Science_Values[Index[["trust"]]]` use those positions to retrieve passages. Because `Science_Values` is a vector, there is no row-and-column comma.

🗣 **Comment:** Read the retrieved passages before interpreting the matches. A word can occur in a reference or notice as well as the main article; a match alone does not establish its meaning.

## Summary {#summary}

In this chapter, you used `str_detect()` to test text and produce logical results, then used those results with `filter()` to select rows. You refined searches with word boundaries, alternation, and capitalization options. These patterns changed what counted as a match without changing the familiar role of a logical test.

You also used `sapply()` to collect row counts and `lapply()` to build a keyword index. The index stores matching positions so you can retrieve passages with brackets. A matching-passage count does not tell you how often a word occurs or what the author means by it. Read the retrieved text to interpret the result.

## Chapter Terms {#chapter-terms}

**Alternation**: Using `|` inside a regular expression to allow either alternative to match.

**Case-insensitive matching**: Matching that ignores differences between uppercase and lowercase letters. In this chapter, `ignore_case = TRUE` enables it.

**Case-sensitive matching**: Matching that treats uppercase and lowercase letters as different.

**Corpus**: A collection of text prepared for analysis. Here, each entry in `Science_Values` is one passage.

**Keyword index**: In this chapter, a named list connecting each keyword with the positions of matching passages.

**[`lapply()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/lapply.html)**: Applies a function to each element of a list or vector and returns a list containing the results.

**Pattern**: Text or a matching rule that describes what to look for in text.

**[`regex()`](https://stringr.tidyverse.org/reference/modifiers.html)**: Sets regular-expression matching options, such as whether capitalization matters. It supplies a pattern to a search function; it does not perform the search itself.

**Regular expression**: A text pattern that can use special symbols, such as `^`, `\\b`, and `|`, to describe matching rules.

**[`sapply()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/lapply.html)**: Applies a function to each element of a list or vector and simplifies the results when possible. In this chapter's row-count example, it returns a vector of counts.

**[`str_detect()`](https://stringr.tidyverse.org/reference/str_detect.html)**: Tests text for a pattern and returns logical results indicating which entries match.

**Word boundary**: A position at the beginning or end of a word. Write `\\b` inside a quoted R pattern to specify one; `"\\bSouth\\b"` matches `South` but not the beginning of `Southampton`.
